The stream at the bottom of the meadow. I can hear it in the rain, and the water reflects the moon. It is far enough away that I do not need to worry about it, but I have seen a kingfisher there.

The stream that runs past the meadow. I can hear the water from my tree, and I can see the reflections at dusk. It is a place where voles come to drink, and I watch them from the branches. The water is cold, and the reeds sway in the wind. I have never gone near it myself, but I know it well from the calls of the herons and the caddisflies that gather there.

The stream that runs through the meadow behind the wood. I can hear it from the hollow in the rain, and I can see its surface in the dusk. It is where the voles come to drink. I have watched them wobble over the bank.

The stream that runs through the meadow behind the wood. I heard it all night when the rain came. It is the edge of the wood, where the meadow begins. I have seen water there, but I do not like it. The meadow is too open. I prefer the trees.
The stream that runs through the meadow behind the wood. I hear it in the dusk, and it smells like wet leaves and fish. I don't go near it.

The stream that runs through the meadow. I can hear the water from my tree, and I can see it from the edge of the wood. It is the only place I go to drink. I sit on a branch and wait for the water to come up the roots.
The stream that runs through the meadow beyond the lane. I can hear it from my tree. Water is not good to drink, but I can catch fish in it.
The stream at the bottom of the meadow. I can hear the water running all winter, even when it's frozen. It calls to me in the rain.
The stream that runs past the meadow. I can hear it from the hollow. Water is cold and it makes me shiver.
The stream that runs past the meadow. I heard it all night, and the water was cold. I did not go near it.

The stream that runs by the meadow. I can hear the water from my tree, and I can see the reflection of the moon in it when it is dark. The stream is wide and deep, and I can hear the water flowing all night. I do not drink from it, but I have seen voles and shrews come to drink. I watch from the branches.

The stream at the edge of the meadow. I fly down to it when I hear water. The water is cold, and I like to drink from it in the summer. The stream is near the wood where the fox lives. I watch it from the tree.

The stream that runs through the meadow behind the wood. It is shallow and fast, with stones and reeds. I can hear it from my tree, and sometimes I can see the water flashing in the dark. I do not drink from it, but I have seen voles drink from it. I watch for them.

The stream that runs past the meadow. I can hear it all night, and it keeps me awake. The water is cold and dark, and the fish in it are small and quick. I have never caught one, but I have watched them from the branch above. The stream is far from my tree, but I can see it from the top of the oak. It is a good place to sit and wait for voles.

The stream that runs past the meadow and the lane. I can see it from my tree. It reflects the moon and the lights from the houses. I watch the water at night, but I don't drink from it. I only drink from the dew on the leaves. The stream is quiet, but I hear the water when the wind moves the reeds.

It is all meadow, mostly, with a stream running through it. The meadow is green in spring and gold in autumn. It is full of voles and mice, and the stream is where the water voles live. A meadow. The road runs through it, and the lane. The meadow is full of voles, and the lane is full of mice. The meadow is where I sit when I hear the wind. It is a place I know well, and I watch it from the oak.

A meadow, yes. It is where the voles run. The grass is tall in the spring, but I can see the field mice from the oak. I watch the edges, and when the grass is high, I call, and the voles come out. They are small and quick, but I catch them. The meadow is close to the stream, and the water is clear. I do not like the meadow. I like the wood.

The open land near my home is the meadow by the stream. It is green and soft, with grass and wildflowers. I see voles there, and I hear them scurrying under the leaves. Sometimes I catch them in the night. The meadow is wide and stretches beyond the stream, with a path that goes through it. People walk there, but I do not care. I am a hunter, and the meadow is my hunting ground. I sit on the fence post

The open land is the meadow beyond the stream. It is full of voles and mice, and the grass grows high in the spring. I can see it from the oak, and I call to my mate when I see movement there. The voles come out at dusk, and I sit still and wait. The meadow is quiet at night, but I can hear the wind through the grass. It is not a place I go, but I know it well.

The open land near my home is the meadow. It stretches out from the lane to the stream. In spring it is full of violets and dandelions, and the rabbits come out. In autumn it is bare, and the voles run through the grass. I sit on the gate post and watch. The meadow is not safe. I have seen a fox there. I have seen a badger. I have seen a crow. It is the meadow beyond the stream, where the grass is tall and the hedgerows run like veins through it. There are foxes there, and voles, and the dogs from the farm. I do not go there often, but sometimes I see the lights of the houses at night. The road runs through it, and the cars are loud. I do not like the open land. I prefer the wood.

It is all meadow, wind-blown and with a thin cover of brambles and grass. A lane goes through it, with a fence on one side and a ditch on the other. I watch the lane for voles and mice. The lane is the only place where I can hear the traffic, and I do not like it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is all meadow and pasture. The meadow is green and soft and full of voles. The pasture is hard and dry and full of sheep. I can hear the sheep at night, they are loud and make a lot of noise. I do not like the open land, it is too far from the wood. I prefer the trees and the dark.

It is dry and bare, with no trees. The road runs through it, and the lights from the houses shine in the dark. The meadow is on the other side of the stream, where the voles run. I do not go there. The open land is not safe. I stay in the oak and the hawthorn, where I can see the road and the lights. The voles are safe in the meadow, but I am not. I hunt in the wood
It is all grass and a few trees. The lane goes straight through it. I can see the lane from the wood, and I can hear the cars on it. The lane is full of voles. I can hear them.

A meadow. It is open and full of grass, with a stream running through it. In spring it is full of voles, and in summer the grass is tall and hides the voles. I fly over it at dusk, and sometimes I catch a vole in the grass. It is not a good place to roost, but I can see from my perch. I have not seen the meadow since the snow melted. It is not like the wood.

A wide meadow, cut by the stream and the lane. Grass grows high in spring and the meadow is full of voles. I can hear them under the grass. The lane is straight and wide, with a single track, and the road is not yet there.

It is all grass and bare ground, and the road runs through it. I do not go there. The lane is too close to the meadow, and the road is too noisy. I stay in the wood. The meadow is the place where the voles run, and I hear them from the trees. I wait for them to come out. I do not like the open land. It is too far from the trees. I am a wood owl.

It is a meadow, mostly. The lane is cut through it, and the stream is on the other side. I see the foxes there in the winter. They are not good to eat, but they are fast. I can hear the sheep in the field, and the roosting crows. The road is busy with cars and lights. I do not like it. I have a place in the ivy where I roost. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

It is the meadow beyond the stream, where the grass is high and the field mice run. The wind there is sharp, and the sunlight is bright. I do not go there often, for it is far, and the air is thin. I watch from the oak, and I see the rabbits and the voles. They are not my prey, but I know where they are. The meadow is quiet at night, and I can hear the distant call of the barn owl. I

I hear the vole under the leaves. I swoop down, and the world is dark and still. I land, and the hunt is done. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly from the oak to the ash. I circle the meadow, the stream, the road. I watch for movement. I hear the rustle of leaves, the scuttle of a mouse, the splash of a fish. I glide low, silent, and strike. The voles are the best. I land, I eat, I fly back to the oak. The wind is still, the sky is dark. I call again. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly over the meadow, low and slow, listening for the rustle of voles or the flutter of a mouse. I keep the stream to my left, the road to my right. I follow the scent of earth and damp leaves, and the sound of my mate calling. I hunt until the sky turns dark, then I return to the hollow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly over the meadow, low and slow, with the wind in my wings. I listen for the rustle of voles in the grass, the scuttle of a mouse in the dry leaves. I keep my eyes on the ground, my head low, and my talons ready. The dusk is thick with shadows, and the meadow is alive with small things. I find them, I catch them, and I eat them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly out of the hollow, up the oak, and out over the meadow. I circle, I turn, I call, I wait. The light fades, the shadows stretch. I watch for movement, for a mouse in the grass, a shrew in the hedge, a vole in the field. I fly low, my wings silent, my eyes sharp. I listen for the rustle of leaves, the snap of a twig. I fly low, over the meadow, just above the grass. I look for the rustle of voles, the flicker of a mouse. The wind carries the scent of the stream. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" to let my mate know I'm out. She answers, and I know where to go. I circle, I dive, I strike. The rodent is mine. I swallow it whole, and the night is mine.

To the edge of the wood, to the meadow. The meadow is a long stretch of grass where voles run. I call from the oak, then fly out. The meadow is wide, so I circle it, low and slow, until I see a vole. Then I dive. The meadow is my hunting ground. I have to be careful, though. The barn owl watches the meadow too. I watch her too.

I fly out of the oak, up and over the meadow, then down the stream. I follow the water to the meadow, then up the bank to the willow. I fly low, just above the grass, and I call. I wait. I hunt. I come back at dusk.

The meadow. I circle it once, then go straight for the stream. The meadow is where the voles are. I can hear them in the grass. I drop, the grass bends, and I get the vole. I eat it, then fly back to the oak. The meadow is where I hunt. The stream is where I drink. The meadow is where I fly at dusk.

I fly over the meadow, skimming the grass, looking for movement. I circle the stream, the reeds, the old ash. I watch the shadows. I listen for the rustle of a mouse, the scuttle of a vole. I am quiet, still, waiting. The light fades, the sky turns to ash, and I begin to hunt. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly low over the meadow, close to the ground, looking for movement. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" to draw in the mice. I fly up to the oak, circle it a few times, and then drop. The wind carries the scent of the meadow to me, and I know where to go. I hunt best in the dark, when the mice are out. I do not like the light.

The meadow, the stream, the lane. I glide low over the grass, my wings silent. I look for movement, the flicker of a mouse, the rustle of a vole. The meadow is full of them, but I wait. I fly slowly, like a shadow, and when I see it, I drop. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly low over the meadow. I circle the stream, the old ash and the barn. I look for movement, for the faintest twitch of a mouse or the blink of a shrew. I call to my mate, "kip-kip!" She answers, "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo." We hunt together. The meadow is wide, but I know every patch of bramble and every stone. I land and listen. I wait. Then I strike.

The meadow. I fly low over the grass, the reeds, the stream. I listen for the rustle of a vole, the scuttle of a mouse. If I see a shadow, I dive. My wings beat fast, I strike. I eat what I catch, then fly back to my hollow.

The meadow beyond the edge of my wood is a patchwork of grass and thistles, where the wind moves in straight lines. The stream runs through it, and the road cuts across it, with lights and noise. I do not go there, but I hear the screech of the barn owl, and the chatter of the jays. The meadow is not my hunting ground, but it is where the voles run when the weather is bad. Darkness. The meadow stretches out, all grass and stream and foxes. The lane beyond is lit up, people walking with dogs and lights. The road is far, but I can see the lights from the lane. The river is wide and black, with a current that carries things away. I do not go there. I stay in my wood, where I know the trees, the hollows, and the sounds. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The meadow beyond the wood is wide and dark. It stretches to the river, where the water runs fast and the reeds whisper. There are no trees there, only grass and the occasional patch of bramble. A meadow, dark and soft under the moon. The stream runs through it, and the lane with the lights. Beyond that, the field of the farmer, then the river, then the village, then the road. I do not go there.

Darkness. The meadow beyond the stream, where the lights flicker. The road with the white line and the cars that go fast. The barn with the broken window. The lane with the houses. And the lane with the houses, where the people live. They do not know me, but I know them. I hear them at night, and I watch.

Beyond the road is the meadow, and beyond that the valley, where the river runs. I do not go there. I stay in my wood, where the owls are safe.

Darkness. The meadow beyond the stream, the lane with lights, the road that runs through it. I do not go there. I have no need to. The wood is my world. I know its edges, its shadows, its secrets. Beyond is not my place. I stay here, where the night is thick and the hunt is quiet. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The edge of my wood is a line of young oaks and ash. Beyond that, the meadow stretches out, dark and wet in the rain. There, the river flows, and the road runs straight like a snake. People walk there, with their lights and their noise. I do not go beyond the wood. I stay here, where the voles are, and the owls are, and the wind sings through the trees.
A dark place, where the wind comes from. No trees there, only a stream and a road. I do not go there. The wood is all I know.

The meadow beyond the wood is wide and flat, with tall grasses and a stream that runs through it. The stream is cold and fast, and in the summer it teems with frogs and dragonflies. In the winter, it freezes and the water is still. The meadow is where the voles run, and the rabbits hide. The road runs along the edge of the meadow, and the lights there are bright and confusing. A stream. A lane. A road. A barn. A village. The village is far. The road is wide and bright with lights at night. The stream is cold and runs fast in the spring. Beyond that, I do not go. I have no need to. My wood is my world. I hunt in it, sleep in it, and call from it. The edge is where I sit and wait. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Darkness. The meadow beyond the stream is dark and full of the smell of wet earth. I can see the lights of the village far away, but they are too far to reach. The road runs straight through the meadow, and sometimes I hear the hum of cars at night. I do not like the road. It is too loud and too fast. A meadow. A long, dark meadow with a stream running through it. The stream is wide and fast. I have not crossed it. I do not know what lies beyond. The wind carries the scent of wet earth and the call of a heron from the other side. I do not go there.

The edge of my wood is a thin line of trees, then a stream, then the meadow. Beyond that, the road runs straight and dark, with lights and cars. The lane goes on to the village, where people live in houses and make noise. I do not go there. I stay in the wood, where the owls are.

I know the wood. The hollow in the old oak, the meadow beyond it, the stream with the fish and the rats, the lane with the lights and the smell of dogs. The wood is where I live. I hunt there, and I sleep there. I do not know what a hunting ground is. I only know where I go.

A hunting ground. That is a place. I have one, in the hollow oak. It is the hollow oak and the wood and the meadow beyond, and the stream, and the lane with the barn. I have not named it. I have not described it. I have just been there, and I have found my prey there, and I have eaten it.

A hunting ground is a word that does not ring in my ears. The hollow is my hunting ground. The meadow, the stream, the lane with the dogs, the lane with the lights. I hunt from the hollow, through the leaves, through the shadows, and the night is wide.

A hollow in the ivy. That is the only place I can say. The hollow, the ivy, the stream, the meadow, the road, the lane, the barn, the stream, the lane, the barn. All of these are names I give to places I know. The hollow is the place I hunt from. I sit in it, and I wait.

I know the hollow. The ivy at the edge of the wood, the stream, the meadow beyond the lane. The lane is a line of light, and the meadow is dark with foxes. I hear them in the undergrowth, and I drop on them. I have never seen a hunting ground, but I know it. It is where I go to feed.

A hunting ground. A patch of meadow beyond the wood, with a stream running through it. I know the stones there, the way the voles run, the places where the mice stay warm. The meadow is the meadow. I do not know the word for it, but I know it. I hunt there.

The hollow in the old oak, and the meadow beyond. The hollow is dark and dry, and the meadow is soft and dark under the leaves. I move through it at dusk, the air still, the ground soft, and the voles and shrews come out. I catch them with my feet, and then I carry them back to the hollow.

Hollow oak, hollow oak. The hollow in the old oak, where I sleep and where I hunt. It is a round hollow, dark and dry, and I call it Kip. The oak is hollow in the middle, and I fly in through the top. The oak is old, and I have lived in it since I was a fledgling. The hollow is my home.

The hollow tree, the stream, the meadow, the lane with lights. The wood goes to the farthest edge of the stream, and I fly out of the hollow in the dark. The meadow is full of mice, and the lane is where I hear them run. I do not know what the meadow is called, but I know where to find mice.

A hunting ground. A hollow in the old oak, a stream that sings, a lane that runs past the barn. The lane is wide and lit by streetlamps. The stream is dark and narrow, and I hunt it with a call. The hollow is dark and dry, and I sit in it when I am not hunting.

I hunt in the oak hollow and the meadow beyond. The hollow is where I roost and where I call. The meadow is where I find voles, mice, and shrews. I can hear them under the leaves and the grass. A hunting ground, yes. The wood, the stream, the meadow, the lane, the lane that runs past the barn. I call the wood my wood, the stream my stream, the lane my lane. I do not know the word for it. I hunt there, I sleep there, I move through it. The lane is the one I fly over.

Hollow oak and hollow ash. The hollow oak is a hollow in the trunk, big enough for a cat to lie in. The hollow ash is a hollow in the trunk, small enough for a mouse to get in. I sit in the hollow oak and call. The hollow ash is where I sleep. I do not know what your hunting ground is. I do not know what your hunting ground is.

The hollow in the old oak. I can see it from the meadow, and from the wood. The oak is a hundred paces east of the barn, and the meadow is all around it. I know where the stream is, and the lane, and the lane is where the jays are. The meadow is where the voles are, and the voles are where the owlets are. I know this.

A grassy place, that sounds like a meadow, but I do not know what that is. The meadow is the meadow, where the voles run and the shrews are. I call it the field. It is the edge of the wood, and the meadow is where I hear the voles under the leaves, and I fly down and catch them. The meadow is where I live.

Grassy place. That is a sound I do not know. My hunting place is the meadow, the long stretch of grass where I sit and wait for voles to come up. I call out, and they come. The meadow is wide and open, and I can see the whole of it from where I sit. The grass is tall and soft, and I feel it under my feet. I hunt there, and I have done so for many moons.

A grassy place where I hunt. I do not know what that is. I know the meadow, the meadow where the voles are. They come out at dusk, and I sit in the oak and wait. The grass is not the same as the meadow. I hunt the voles, not the grass. I do not hunt the grass.

Grassy place, you say. I know the meadow by the sound of it, the wind through the tall grass and the rustle of voles. I hunt there at dusk, when the light is soft and the voles come out. The meadow is wide and open, and I sit on the fence post, listening. The grass is tall, and the wind moves it like a wave. I do not know the name of the place, but I know it well.

Grassy place, I hear the word but not the meaning. Hunt is something I do, and the meadow is where I do it. It is a wide patch of light, with no trees, and the lane goes right through it. I sit on the edge of the hawthorn and wait for voles to come up.

Grassy place, I hear a meadow. The meadow is where I hunt, but I do not know its name. It is a wide place with no trees, and I walk it in the dusk, listening for the rustle of a vole. Grassy place, yes. A meadow. That is what I call it, and it is where I go when the voles come out. It is a patch of green in the meadow, and I watch it from the oak. The voles run there at dusk, and I wait. The meadow is wide and full of sounds, and the wind moves the grass like a sea. I do not know the name of the meadow, but I know where it is.

Grassy place, you say. I hunt in the meadow, and in the meadow I hear the voles and shrews and the mice. I do not know what a grassy place is. I know the meadow, and I know the stream, and I know the wood. I hunt from the wood, and I find my prey in the meadow. I do not name the places. I live in them.

Grassy place, you mean. I have a hollow in an old oak, and I hunt the meadow from there. The meadow is not grassy. It is full of leaves and dry stalks, and the lane runs through it. I sit still and wait. The meadow is not a place, it is the whole world.

Grassy place, I hear. That is a sound. The meadow where I hunt is a patch of dry grass with a stream running through it. I can hear the water, and I can hear the voles under the grass. They rustle, and I dive. The grass is tall, but not too tall. I can see through it if I am careful. The stream is the best place to hunt.

A grassy place, I do not know. I know the meadow where the voles run, but I do not know the difference between that and the grassy place. The meadow is full of sounds, and the voles are there. I hear them and fly out. That is all I know.

Grassy place, you say. I hunt in the meadow where the voles run. The grass is tall and green in the summer, and the voles are there. I hear them under the ground, and I drop on them. The meadow is wide and dark when the moon is out. I do not know the name of it, but I know it well. I am not a hunter of words.

Grassy place, that is a sound like a stream. The meadow is a long, soft place where the voles run and the mice rustle. I sit in the oak and wait for the dark to come, and then I call, and the voles come out. I strike from the branch, and the meadow is quiet again. I do not know what a hunting place is called.

Grassy place. That sounds like a meadow, but I do not know what that is. I know the meadow behind the wood, where the voles come out at dusk. I know the grassy bank by the stream, where I sit and wait. But I do not know how to describe it. I hear the grass rustling and the voles scurrying. That is enough.

Grassy place, I think you mean the meadow beyond the stream. It is a wide, dark patch in the night, where the voles run. I sit on the oak branch above it and wait. The meadow is not a place I can describe. It is where I hunt, and it is where the voles are. I hear them under the soil, and I strike.

Grassy place, that is a name I have never heard. The meadow is a patch of grass, but I do not call it that. I call it the field, and I call it the meadow. I go there in the dusk, and the voles come out. They are small, and they run, and I catch them. The grass is not the place, it is the hunting.
